newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-$8 bln deal aims to create "new ICI".
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-$8 bln deal aims to create "new ICI".

text.p: Imperial Chemical Industries Plc said on Wednesday it was buying Unilever Plc's speciality chemicals business for $8 billion in a move to create a "new ICI".
The purchase continues a metamorphosis which began with the demerger of ICI's pharmaceuticals arm Zeneca Group Plc in 1993.

In a single strategic purchase, ICI achieved its objective of shifting its emphasis towards higher-margin speciality light chemicals and away from the more cyclical and low margin heavy-end of the market.
ICI's deal has also given it widespread presence in the key Asia-Pacific market, where Unilever's speciality chemicals units have already built fast-growing and profitable operations.

Sir Ronald Hampel, ICI chairman, said the acquisition would create "a new ICI for the new century" and told a news conference that he was "dead certain the next five years will be better" in terms of share performance. The deal will be fully earnings-enhancing by 1998.
Shares in the chemicals giant were up by 32 pence to 746 1/2 by 1500 GMT, with Unilever up two at 1649 1/2.
Analysts also welcomed the news. Paul Satchell at Paribas told Reuters he regarded the deal as positive. "It is a bold move in the right direction," he said.

The four units ICI bought from Unilever are National Starch, a world leader in industrial adhesives and speciality starches; Quest, one of the world's leading fragrance, food and flavour companies; Unichema, which is in oleochemicals and Crosfield which makes silicates, zeolites and silicas.
"The purchase will create a formidable force in speciality chemicals," said Charles Miller Smith, ICI chief executive.

The deal will be financed through debt which ICI plans to reduce gradually through a three billion pound ($5 billion) divestment programme which includes the sale of a 62.4 percent stake in ICI Australia.
Satchell ICI had paid a full price but noted that the group promised to bring down its debt levels quickly.
This should be helped by cash from the purchased units. They generated $1 billion in three years after capital expenditure of $200 million per annum, said the ICI finance director Alan Spall.
Unilever first made a "pre-emptive strike" for Unilever's speciality chemicals division a year ago, said Miller Smith, who was a Unilever boss during the 1980s.
It was rebuffed the first time because Unilever was still reviewing its options but persistence paid off.
Miller Smith's knowledge of the businesses from his past Unilever tenure as finance chief helped ICI to clinch a speedy and favourable conclusion, Hampel said.
Hampel was confident that further strides could be made in sales under the ICI banner.
"We see significant upside," said Hampel. "I'd be very disappointed if we don't see faster sales growth than the six to seven percent per annum seen recently."
One new customer ICI has its eyes on is Proctor and Gamble Co, the U.S. rival of Unilever which remains virgin sales territory.
The group also sees a change in its culture, with the absorption of the Unilever units fostering a "more international and entrepreneurial culture".
The deal is seen providing a good fit, with few areas of overlap, say analysts. Synergy costs would result in a charge of 50 million pounds, said one analyst.
Analysts see all the acquisitions as good buys in light of their track record.

The businesses being bought had a 10 year profit record, with profitability up 40 percent between 1987 and 1990, maintained during the 1990-1993 recession and rising a further 73 percent between 1993 and 1996. ($ = 0.611 British Pounds)
